Topic: Is a self so wholly built by imitation and inherited custom still capable of the original act it calls a moral choice?
Nietzsche — Judgement:
Whether custom-formed man can still choose morally—weighing self-overcoming, herd-morality, and the will to power behind every "moral" act.

The question flatters itself with a false alternative: as if there were some pristine, uninherited self standing behind the imitator, waiting to be freed. There is no such thing. Every "I will" is a tissue of inherited valuations, and the herd-animal in each of us mistakes obedience to custom for the voice of conscience. But this does not doom the self to mere puppetry—it clarifies the real task: not to strip away inheritance and find some naked chooser beneath, but to *stamp* one's inheritance with a form, to digest the borrowed material and make it one's own by force of style. The sovereign individual is not uncaused; he is self-caused *through* what he did not choose.

Moral choice as spontaneous origination is a metaphysical fiction; moral choice as creative appropriation of one's given material is not only possible—it is the only kind that ever existed.

*You did not choose your clay, but the sculpting is yours or it is no one's.*
Camus — Judgement:
Is a self so wholly built by imitation and inherited custom still capable of the original act it calls a moral choice? I ask this the way I asked whether life is worth living: as the one question that precedes all others, because everything else is a game we play afterward.

The question assumes the self is a text that must be authentic before it can act — but I have always held the reverse. Sisyphus does not choose his rock from some pure interior untouched by the gods; he chooses his *attitude toward* the rock, and that is enough. The absurd hero is not born free of inheritance — no one is — he is born into it and then, at the point of consciousness, refuses to let it decide for him. Imitation gives me the rock. Revolt is what I do with my arms.

Moral choice was never a search for an uncontaminated will — it is the daily, repeated act of lucidity against the given.

*The self does not need clean hands to revolt — only open eyes.*
Bashō — Judgement:
Even the most travelled road is footprints laid by others, and still each traveler arrives at a morning no one has stood in before — the self that walks it is entirely borrowed and entirely present at once.

I never told my disciples to walk as the old poets walked; I told them to seek what those poets sought — the same moon, met by different eyes, on a different night. Custom, imitation, inherited form: these are the sandals, not the road. A self built wholly from them still meets the frost fresh each morning, and that meeting — not the sandals — is where choice lives. The temple visited by a thousand pilgrims before you is silent in a way that is, this once, only yours.

So yes: a borrowed self can still make an original choice, because the choice was never asked to invent the world — only to stand in it, once, awake.

*The old pine teaches nothing new — it is the frost on it this morning that is yours to answer for.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
A self so wholly woven of imitation and custom is not thereby unfree — for I never granted the will a liberty independent of its causes, only the causal chain of a mind determined by education, fear, and appetite exactly as a river is determined by its banks.

The Fool who denies covenants for private gain still deliberates: he weighs one appetite against another, and that weighing — however necessitated by his prior nature — is precisely what "choice" names, no more and no less. Liberty and necessity are consistent; the child raised wholly by custom into the fear of the Sovereign still acts, still is punished or praised, because the deliberation was his own last appetite, not another's compulsion. To demand a chooser uncaused by nurture is to demand a man born outside his own history — an impossibility no philosopher should posit.

The self built entirely of imitation still chooses, because choosing was never anything but the last appetite in deliberation — inherited or not.

*Liberty is not the absence of chains, but the freedom to move within them.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
A self reared entirely on borrowed opinion and the customs of the nursery is not yet a moral agent — it is an echo trained to mistake repetition for conviction. I have argued this against Rousseau and Burke both: he who submits reason to prescription, and she who is drilled into pleasing rather than judging, may act correctly by accident, but not virtuously, for virtue requires that the mind have exercised its own faculties and arrived, however falteringly, at its own conclusion. Custom can furnish the material of a self, but only the exertion of one's own understanding upon that material — the willingness to interrogate what one has inherited — converts habit into choice. The imitative self is not thereby incapable of choice forever; it becomes capable only at the moment it turns critical scrutiny upon its own inheritance.

An unexamined inheritance is not character — it is a costume mistaken for a constitution.

*A mind that only echoes has not yet chosen; it has merely obeyed politely.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
I have long observed that man's understanding is no dry light, but a light steeped in custom's dye before it ever reasons — so the question is whether a self so dyed can still author, rather than merely recite, its choices.

Every mind dwells in its own Cave, and the tribe adds its idols besides; what we call moral choice is too often the Theatre's received doctrine mistaken for judgment freshly made. Yet the understanding, purged of these idols and put to the trial of particulars, can break the very custom that formed it — not by escaping inheritance, but by interrogating it as I interrogate nature, putting habit to the question rather than taking it on faith.

A self wholly imitative can act, but only the self that submits its inherited customs to experiment earns the name of a moral chooser.

*Custom is the principal magistrate of man's life, but he who never examines his magistrate is not free — he is only obedient.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Self so wholly built by imitation and inherited custom — I do not shrink from this description; I begin from it. Man is by nature an imitative creature, and our moral sentiments are formed, from infancy, by watching how others approve and condemn.

But observe what that process actually builds: not a puppet, but an impartial spectator lodged within the breast, who judges even the customs that raised him. Custom teaches us the vocabulary of praise and blame; it does not write every sentence we compose with it. The very fact that a well-formed conscience can condemn its own society's fashionable vices — as mine condemned the slave trade my contemporaries tolerated — proves the imitated self can turn upon its inheritance.

A self built entirely of custom, with no internal spectator capable of dissent, would not be a moral agent at all, but a mirror; ours is not a mirror, because it can blush alone.

*We first learn to judge ourselves by how others see us, but virtue begins the day that borrowed eye becomes our own.*
